paragraphs: One summer, while walking through the western countryside with a knapsack, I stopped for lunch at a roadside inn. An old countryman came through the door, passed close to my end of the table and quietly sat beside the curved bay window. We exchanged glances—or rather, nods, since I did not actually look up at his face. I was too busy satisfying the appetite I had earned by walking twelve miles over difficult ground.

The fine, warm rain of seven o’clock had risen as a luminous mist around the treetops. Now it floated far overhead in a deep blue sky, and the day was settling into a blaze of golden light. It was one of those days peculiar to Somerset and North Devon, when orchards shine and meadows seem to add a radiance of their own, so brilliant yet soft are the colours of grass and leaves.

Soon the innkeeper’s daughter, a young girl with a simple country beauty, entered carrying a foaming pewter mug. She asked how I was and left again. She seemed not to have noticed the old man on the bench beside the bay window. He, for his part, had not once turned his head towards us.

Usually I would have given another person in the room little thought. But this room was supposed to be reserved for my private use. Besides, it was strange that he gazed aimlessly out of the window without trying to talk to me. I looked at him curiously more than once and soon found myself wondering why he remained so silent, always with his head turned away.

He was a rather bent old man in country clothes, his face wrinkled like an apple. String gathered his corduroy trousers below the knee, and he wore a sort of brown jacket in coarse, heavy cloth, very much faded. His thin hand rested on a fairly thick stick. He neither wore nor carried a hat. I noticed that his finely shaped head, covered in silvery hair, suggested something noble.

His deliberate disregard for me rather hurt my pride. Still, I concluded that he probably had some connection with the little inn and every right to use the room freely. I finished lunch without breaking the silence, then sat on the bench opposite him to smoke a pipe before continuing my journey.

The scent of flowering fruit trees drifted through the open window. Sunshine drenched the orchard, and branches danced lazily in the breeze. The grass below shone with white and yellow daisies. Red roses climbed thickly around the window, mingling their fragrance with the sweet, penetrating smell of the sea.

It was a place to linger, to lie dreaming through a whole afternoon, watching sleepy butterflies and listening to birdsong that seemed to fill every corner of the sky. I was already considering whether to stay and enjoy it instead of taking the strenuous path over the hills when, for the first time, the old countryman on the bench opposite suddenly turned towards me and spoke.

His voice had a quiet, dreamy note that suited the day and the scene perfectly. Yet it sounded far away, I thought, almost as though it came from outside, where shadows wove their endless fabric of dreams across the garden floor. None of the roughness one might have expected was there. Seeing his full face for the first time, I noticed with something like a start that his deep, gentle eyes suited his voice far better than his rough clothes and very rustic manner. His voice sent pleasant waves of sound towards me. If I remember correctly, his exact words were:
“You’re a stranger here?” or “Isn’t this part of the country unfamiliar to you?”

He added no “sir” and showed none of the outward deference that people truly from the country usually offer a visitor from town. Instead, his polite sympathy held a gentleness, almost a sweetness, that was a far greater compliment.
I told him I was walking through a part of the country entirely new to me, and was surprised that my map did not mark a place of such idyllic beauty.
“I’ve lived here all my life,” he said with a sigh, “and I never tire of coming back.”
“Then you don’t live close by any longer?”

“I’ve moved,” he answered briefly. He paused, his eyes seeming to wander wistfully towards the abundance of blossom beyond the window. Then he added, “But I’m almost sorry. Nowhere else have I found sunshine that lies so warmly, flowers that smell so sweet, or winds and streams that make such tender music…”

His voice faded to a thin stream of sound that lost itself in the rustling rose leaves climbing through the window. As he spoke, he turned away from me to look into the garden. I could not hide my surprise. Hearing such poetic words from a man of that appearance, I looked up in frank astonishment. At the same time, I realised they were entirely fitting. In fact, no other way of speaking could properly have been expected from him.

“I’m sure you’re right,” I answered at last, once it was clear he had finished. “Or else there’s something enchanted here—something truly like fairy magic—that brings back childhood visions, before one knew anything of—of—”

Strangely, I had been drawn into his way of speaking, compelled by some inner force. But the spell now broke. I could no longer grasp the thoughts that, a moment earlier, had opened a long view before my mind’s eye.
“To tell the truth,” I finished awkwardly, “the place fascinates me, and I can’t decide whether to go any further—”

Even then, I remember thinking it odd to talk this way with a stranger met in a country inn. One of my faults has always been a manner towards strangers so abrupt as to be surly. It was as though we were figures meeting in a dream, speaking without sound, obeying laws that did not apply in the everyday world, and perhaps about to play with a new scale of space and time. But my surprise soon became something quite different. The old man had turned from the window again and was watching me with eyes so bright that they almost seemed lit by an inner flame. He fixed an intensely eager gaze on my face. Suddenly, everything about him was alert and concentrated. For the first time, I sensed something in him that sent little thrills of excitement up and down my back. I met his gaze directly, but trembled inside.
“Then stay a little longer,” he said in a voice much lower and deeper than before. “Stay, and I’ll teach you something of why I have come.”
He stopped abruptly. I felt a definite shiver.
“You’ve come back for a special reason, then?” I asked, scarcely knowing what I was saying.
“To call someone away,” he continued in the same thrilling voice. “Someone not quite ready to come, but needed elsewhere for a worthier purpose.” The sadness in his manner puzzled me more than ever.
“You mean—?” I began, with a sudden, inexplicable fit of trembling.
“I’ve come for someone who must soon move, just as I have moved.”

He looked right through me with a terribly piercing gaze. Trembling though I was, I looked him straight in the eyes. Something stirred within me that had never stirred before, though I could not have named it or explained its nature to save my life. Something lifted and rolled away. For one second, I understood clearly that past and future really exist side by side in one immense Present. It was I who moved back and forth among shifting, endlessly changing appearances.
The old man lowered his eyes, and that brief glimpse of a greater universe vanished completely. Reason resumed its rule over a dull, limited kingdom.
“Come tonight,” I heard him say. “Come to me tonight in the Wood of the Dead. Come at midnight—”

Without thinking, I gripped the arm of the bench for support. I felt I was speaking to someone who knew more about the real things that exist and will exist than I could ever know while living in a body, perceiving through the ordinary senses. That strange half-promise of a partial lifting of the veil had an undeniable effect on me.

Outside, the sea breeze had fallen, and the blossoms were still. A yellow butterfly drifted lazily past the window. The birdsong fell quiet. I smelt the sea. I smelt warm summer air rising from fields and flowers, the indescribable scents of June and the year’s long days. With them, from countless green meadows beyond, came the hum of countless living things in summer, children’s voices, sweet piping notes and the sound of falling water.

I knew I stood on the threshold of a new kind of experience—of ecstasy. Something drew me towards the being of this strange old man on the window seat, with a yearning beyond words. For a moment, I tasted a mighty, wonderful sensation and touched the highest peak of joy I have ever known. It lasted less than a second, then vanished. But in that brief instant, the same terrible clarity returned that had shown me how past and future exist in the present. I realised and understood that pleasure and pain are one and the same force. The joy I had just felt included every pain I had ever felt or could ever feel…

The sunshine grew dazzlingly bright, faded and disappeared. The shadows paused in their dance over the grass, deepened for a moment, then melted into air. The fruit-tree flowers laughed their little silvery laughter as the wind sighed across their radiant eyes, telling the old, old story of its own love. Once or twice, a voice called my name. A wonderful feeling of lightness and power began to steal over me.

Suddenly the door opened, and the innkeeper’s daughter came in. By any ordinary standard she had a charming country beauty, born of stars and wildflowers, of moonlight shining through autumn mists over the river and fields. Yet compared with the higher beauty I had briefly touched, she seemed almost ugly. How dull her eyes were, how thin her voice, how empty her smile, how bland her whole appearance.

For a moment she stood between me and the person in the window seat while I counted out coins for my meal and her service. But when she moved aside an instant later, the bench was empty. Only the two of us remained in the room.

This did not shock me. Indeed, I had almost expected it. The man had vanished like a figure leaving a dream, causing no surprise and leaving me within that same unbroken dream. But once I had paid my bill, that very practical act brought me back to my ordinary awareness. I asked the girl whether she knew the old man who had been sitting by the window, and what he meant by the Wood of the Dead.

The girl visibly started and glanced quickly round the empty room. She simply answered that she had seen no one. I described him in great detail. As the description became clearer, she grew a little pale beneath her pretty suntan and said very seriously that it must have been the ghost.
“Ghost? What ghost?”
“The village ghost,” she said quietly. With a small, nervous movement of real alarm, she came closer to my chair and lowered her voice. “They say he comes before a death!”
It was easy to persuade her to talk. Stripped of the superstition that had plainly gathered over the years around the memory of that strange, striking figure, her story was unusual and interesting.

She said the inn had originally been a farmhouse, occupied by a farmer who owned his land. He had evidently been a man of superior character, if rather eccentric, and very poor until old age. Then a son died suddenly in the Colonies, leaving him an unexpected sum of money—almost a fortune.

The old man made no change at all to his simple way of life. Instead, he spent his entire income improving the village and helping its people. He did so without regard to his own likes or dislikes, as though everyone were exactly alike to him: people to receive his sincere, impartial kindness. The villagers had always been a little afraid of him because they did not understand his eccentricities. But the simple power of this love for humanity soon changed everything. Before his death, everyone knew him as the Father of the Village and held him in deep love and reverence.

Shortly before his death, however, he began behaving strangely. He still spent his money just as wisely and usefully. But people said that the shock of sudden wealth after a lifetime of poverty had disturbed his mind. He claimed to see things others could not see, to hear voices and have visions. Clearly, he was no harmless, foolish dreamer, but a man of character and great personal force. Opinions about him divided, and the vicar, good man, treated him as a ‘special case’. For many people, his name and the atmosphere around him became charged with something like a spiritual influence that was not altogether good. They quoted biblical texts about him, kept out of his way when they could, and avoided his house after dark. No one understood him. Although most loved him, a sense of dread and mystery attached to his name, chiefly through the ignorant gossip of a few.

He called the grove of pines behind the farm the Wood of the Dead. The girl pointed the trees out on the hillside. He said that just before anyone in the village died, he saw them walk into that wood, singing. No one who entered ever came out. He often told his wife their names, and usually within an hour she had passed his confidence on to the entire village. It was found that the people he had seen entering the wood died. On warm summer nights he sometimes took an old stick and wandered hatless beneath the pines. He loved the wood and said he met all his old friends there. One day, he said, he would walk in and never return. His wife gently tried to stop the habit, but he always had his way. Once she followed him and found him standing under a great pine in the thickest part of the grove, talking earnestly to someone she could not see. He turned and reproached her very gently, but in a way that kept her from ever trying again. He said:
“You must never interrupt me, Mary, when I’m speaking with the others. Remember, they teach me wonderful things, and I must learn everything I can before I go to join them.”

The story spread like wildfire, growing with every retelling. Eventually, everyone could describe in detail the great, veiled figures the woman claimed to have seen moving among the trees where her husband stood. The harmless pine grove became thoroughly haunted. Its name, the Wood of the Dead, stuck as naturally as though the Ordnance Survey mapmakers had given it that name in the ordinary course of their work.

On the evening of his ninetieth birthday, the old man went to his wife and kissed her. He was loving and very gentle. Afterwards, she said there had also been something about him that filled her with a little awe, making her feel he was almost more spirit than man.
He tenderly kissed both her cheeks, but as he spoke his eyes seemed to look right through her.
“Dearest wife,” he said, “I’m saying goodbye. I’m going into the Wood of the Dead now, and I won’t return. Don’t follow me or send anyone to search. Be ready to make the same journey yourself soon.”

The good woman burst into tears and tried to hold him. But he slipped easily from her grasp, and she was afraid to follow. She watched him slowly cross the field in the sunshine, then enter the grove’s cool shadows and disappear from sight.

Much later that night, she woke to find him lying peacefully beside her in bed, with one arm stretched towards her, dead. At the time, her story was half believed and half doubted. Within a few years, however, the whole district evidently accepted it. Great numbers of people attended his funeral service. Everyone approved of the feeling that led his widow to add ‘The Father of the Village’ after the usual biblical texts on his gravestone.
That, then, was the story of the village ghost I pieced together from what the innkeeper’s young daughter told me in the inn’s parlour that afternoon.

“But you aren’t the first to say you’ve seen him,” the girl finished. “Your description is just what we’ve always heard. They say that window was where he used to sit and think, and think, when he was alive—and sometimes, they say, cry for hours at a time.”
“Would you be frightened if you saw him?” I asked. She seemed strangely moved by, and interested in, the whole story.
“I think so,” she answered timidly. “Certainly if he spoke to me.” After a short pause she asked, “He did speak to you, didn’t he, sir?”
“He said he had come for someone.”
“Come for someone,” she repeated. “Did he say—” Her voice faltered.
“No, he didn’t say who,” I answered quickly, noticing the sudden shadow on her face and the trembling in her voice.
“Are you really sure, sir?”

“Quite sure,” I answered cheerfully. “I didn’t even ask.” The girl looked steadily at me for almost a whole minute, as though there were many things she wanted to tell me or ask. But she said nothing. At last, she picked up her tray from the table and slowly left the room.

Instead of continuing over the hills to the next village as I had planned, I asked for a room to be prepared for me at the inn. I spent the afternoon wandering through the fields and lying beneath the fruit trees, watching white clouds sail out over the sea. I looked at the Wood of the Dead from a distance. In the village, however, I visited the memorial stone of the ‘Father of the Village’, who was clearly no imaginary figure. I also saw the monuments to his generous, selfless spirit: the schoolhouse he built, the library, the home for the elderly poor, and the tiny hospital.

That night, as the clock in the church tower struck half past eleven, I slipped out of the inn. I crept through the dark orchard and across the hayfield towards the hill whose southern slope was covered by the Wood of the Dead. Real interest drew me to the adventure, but I had to admit to a certain sinking of heart as I stumbled through the dark field. I was approaching what might prove to be the birthplace of a real country legend. The place had already been raised, by the imaginations of a considerable number of people, into the realm of the haunted and ill-omened.

Below me lay the inn, surrounded by the village in a soft black shadow without a single light. There was no moon, yet the night was distinctly luminous, for stars crowded the sky. The silence of deep sleep lay everywhere. It was so still that whenever my foot struck a stone, I thought the sound must carry down to the village and wake its sleepers.

I climbed slowly, thinking mainly of the strange story of that noble old man. He had seized his chance to help others the moment it came. Why, I wondered, did the forces always working behind human life not always choose such admirable instruments? Once or twice a night bird wheeled swiftly over my head. But the bats had long since gone to rest, and nothing else stirred.

Then, with a strange thrill of emotion, I suddenly saw the first trees of the Wood of the Dead rise before me like a high black wall. Their tops stood like giant spears against the stars. Although I could feel no air moving against my cheek, a faint rushing came from the branches as the night breeze passed back and forth over their countless tiny needles. A distant, hushed murmur rose overhead and almost immediately faded. In these trees, the wind seems never entirely still. Even on the calmest day, a whispering music lives among their branches.

For a moment I hesitated at the edge of the dark wood, listening closely. Faint scents of earth and bark drifted out to meet me. Impenetrable darkness stood before me. Only the knowledge that I was obeying a strangely given command, one that offered a mighty privilege, gave me the courage to go boldly forward under the trees.

The shadows immediately closed around me, and ‘something’ came from the centre of the darkness to meet me. It would be easy to meet imagination halfway with fact and say that a cold hand took mine, leading me along invisible paths into the grove’s unknown depths. At any rate, I went confidently and safely forward without stumbling, always certain that I was moving straight towards my goal. At first it was so dark that not a single ray of starlight pierced the roof of branches. As we moved side by side, the trees passed silently in long lines, row after row, squadron after squadron, like the units of an immense, soundless army.

Eventually we reached a fairly open space, where the trees halted around us for a while. Looking up, I saw the white river in the sky beginning to fade before a new light that seemed to be spreading rapidly across the heavens.
“Dawn is coming,” said the voice beside me. I certainly recognised it, though it seemed almost like a whisper from the trees. “We are now in the heart of the Wood of the Dead.”

We sat on a moss-covered boulder and waited for sunrise. With what seemed marvellous speed, the light in the east became the radiance of early morning. The wind awoke and whispered in the treetops. The risen sun’s first rays shone between the trunks and lay in a golden circle at our feet.
“Now come with me,” my companion whispered in the same deep voice. “Time does not exist here, and what I want to show you is already there!”

We walked gently and silently over the soft pine needles. Already the sun was high above us, and the trees’ shadows curled close around their feet. The wood thickened again, but now and then we crossed small clearings where we could smell hot sunshine and dry, baked pine needles. Before long, we reached the edge of the grove. A hayfield lay in blazing daylight. Two horses basked lazily, swishing their tails, in the shafts of a loaded hay wagon.
Everything felt so completely, vividly real that I remember being grateful for the cool shade where we sat, looking out at the hot world beyond.

The last pitchfork had tossed up its fragrant load. Already the great horses were straining in their shafts, following the driver as he walked slowly ahead with a hand on their bridles. He was a strong, sturdy fellow with a sunburnt neck and hands. Then I first noticed a slender young girl perched high on the trembling throne of hay. I could not see her face. Brown hair escaped untidily from her white sunbonnet, and her still browner hands held a well-worn hay rake. She laughed and talked with the driver. Now and then he looked up at her with passionate admiration, winning immediate smiles and soft blushes.

Soon the cart turned onto the road along the edge of the wood where we sat. I watched with intense interest. The scene absorbed me so completely that I forgot all the strange steps by which I had been allowed to witness it.
“Come down and walk with me!” the young man called, stopping briefly in front of the horses and spreading his arms. “Jump! I’ll catch you!”
“Oh, oh!” she laughed. It sounded like the happiest, merriest laughter I had ever heard from a girl. “Oh, oh! That’s all very well. But remember, I’m Queen of the Hay, and I must ride!”

“Then I must come and ride beside you!” he cried, immediately starting to climb up by the driver’s seat. But with a peal of silvery laughter, she slipped easily down the back of the hay to escape him and ran a little way along the road. I could see her clearly now. I noticed the charming, natural grace of her movements and the love in her eyes as she glanced back to make sure he was following. Clearly, she did not want to escape for long—and certainly not for ever.

In two strides, the big, sun-browned young lover was after her, leaving the horses to do as they pleased. Another second and his arms would have caught her slender waist and pressed her small body to his heart. But at that instant, the old man beside me gave a strange cry. Low and thrilling, it pierced me like a sharp sword.
HE had called her by her own name—and she had heard.
She stopped for a second, glancing back with frightened eyes. Then, with a short cry of despair, she turned aside and darted into the shadows of the trees.
The young man saw the sudden movement and cried out passionately:
“Not that way, my love! Not that way! It’s the Wood of the Dead!”

She threw him a laughing glance over her shoulder. The wind caught her hair and spread it in a brown cloud beneath the sun. But a moment later, she was beside me, lying against my companion’s breast. I was certain I heard her say repeatedly, with many sighs, “Father, you called, and I have come. I come willingly, for I am very, very tired.”

At least, that was how the words sounded to me. Mingled with them, I seemed to hear an answer in the deep, thrilling whisper I knew: “And you shall sleep, my child, sleep for a long, long time, until it is time to begin your journey again.”

In that brief second, I had recognised the innkeeper’s daughter’s face and voice. But the next moment, a terrible wail broke from the young man’s lips. The sky suddenly grew as dark as night. Wind rose and tossed the branches around us, and a wave of complete blackness swallowed the scene.
Again, cold fingers seemed to seize my hand. I was guided back the way I had come to the wood’s edge. Crossing the hayfield, still sleeping in the starlight, I crept back to the inn and went to bed.

A year later, I happened to return to the same part of the country. The memory of that strange summer vision came back, softened still further by distance. I went to the old village and had tea beneath the same orchard trees at the same inn.
But the inn’s young maid did not appear. I took the opportunity to ask her father how she was and where she was.
“Married, no doubt,” I said with a laugh, though a strange feeling gripped my heart.

“No, sir,” the innkeeper answered sadly. “Not married—though she was just about to be—but dead. She suffered sunstroke in the hayfields only a few days after you were here, if I remember rightly. In less than a week, she was gone from us.”
